t: Forensic medicine and forensic medical examination
n: This lecture is devoted to forensic medicine and forensic medical examination. Forensic medicine is a distinct medical science that studies the medico-biological questions arising in the work of the courts, investigation and inquiry bodies. It is a body of scientific knowledge on establishing, examining and evaluating medical facts that serve as a source of evidence for law-enforcement agencies. An investigation that ends with the drawing up of an expert's conclusion is called a forensic medical examination.

An examination has four features. First, the investigation is carried out by a specialist who uses knowledge and skills in the field of science, technology or art. Second, it is carried out on a specific task, usually for the purpose of evaluation. Third, the procedure is strictly defined. Fourth, the process and results are documented formally. Remember: the performer, the task, the procedure and the document; these four distinguish an examination from an ordinary investigation.

The subject of forensic medicine is the theory and practice of forensic medical examination. The system of the subject was first scientifically substantiated and proposed in 1948 by M. I. Avdeev. V. L. Popov expressed a view on the structure of the science in 1999: within it he distinguishes the doctrines of death and postmortem changes, of injuries, and of personal identification. That is, the subject of the science is closely tied to the theory and practice of examination.

The subject system consists of eight sections. The first three include the history of development, the organisational and procedural questions of examination, and impairment of health and death from external factors. The fourth to sixth are inspection and examination of the dead body, examination of living persons, and examination of physical evidence. The seventh and eighth sections are devoted to examination on investigation and court materials and to professional offences of medical staff. This is the Avdeev system.

The current components of the science include history, organisational and procedural foundations, forensic thanatology, traumatology, obstetrics and gynaecology, toxicology and biology. The effects of various external factors and the identification of persons and of the injuring instrument are also included. An important change: in 2002, "Professional offences of medical staff" separated as a distinct discipline, namely "Legal foundations of medical practice".

Links with other sciences. Forensic medicine is not a fundamental but an applied science; it is linked with the medical, legal, natural and philosophical sciences. Without mastering the fundamental medical sciences, no forensic medical examination can be carried out. In some cases clinical sciences are also needed: in mechanical injuries, knowledge of traumatology; in criminal abortion, obstetrics and gynaecology; and in eye injuries, ophthalmology.

t: Clinical specialty and the expert's approach
n: Clinical specialty and the expert's approach. A forensic medical specialist cannot have complete knowledge of all medical specialties. The clinician looks from the standpoint of medical care, that is, diagnosis, treatment and prevention. The expert approaches circumstances for the purpose of legal evaluation. In addition, toxicology is linked with chemistry, and external factors, that is, temperature, electric current and atmospheric pressure, with physics.

Principles of examination. The law recognises the principles of legality, respect for human rights and freedoms, independence of the expert, objectivity, comprehensiveness and completeness. The expert works only within the limits of his competence, and personal responsibility for the investigation and conclusion rests with him. The period for identification of objects is also taken into account: abrasions and bruises are best examined within the first 10–15 days.

Objects and methods of examination. Objects: the dead body, living persons, physical evidence, and materials of criminal and civil cases. Methods fall into three groups. General scientific methods include observation, description, comparison and measurement. Particular methods are morphological, radiological and chromatographic. Special methods are used to establish the identity of a person and of the injuring instrument, for example photographic comparison.

History of the ancient period. In Sparta in the 9th–8th centuries BC, the "laws of Lycurgus" noted the need for medical examination in certain cases; Hippocrates, 460–370 BC, also took part in this. After the murder of Julius Caesar in 44 BC, his body was examined by the physician Antistius: of 23 wounds only one was fatal. The Code of Justinian, 6th century, specifies the involvement of physicians and midwives, and states that their conclusion is more important than the testimony of witnesses.

t: The Middle Ages and the Renaissance
n: The Middle Ages and the Renaissance. In 1247 in China, Song Ci published the work "Xi Yuan Lu": it covers the procedure for examining a body, weapons, strangulation, drowning and poisons. In the 13th century in Bologna, Hugh of Lucca gave opinions before the tribunal. The first official forensic examination of a body was carried out in the 14th century in Montpellier. In 1532 in Germany, the legal code "Carolina" noted that physicians must take part in cases of murder, poisoning and the like.

Formation of the science. A separate part of the work of the French surgeon Ambroise Paré is devoted to forensic questions: wounds, asphyxia, carbon monoxide and lightning. At the end of the 16th and the beginning of the 17th century, forensic medicine began to form as an independent science; the names of F. Fidelis and P. Zacchia are mentioned in this connection. In 1681, I. Schreyer applied the lung test to the body of a newborn. In the work of I. Bohn, it was proposed to call the science "forensic medicine".

Scientists of the 19th and 20th centuries. In the 19th century, R. Virchow, K. Rokitansky, E. von Hofmann, P. Brouardel, S. A. Gromov, P. A. Minakov, I. I. Neiding and others made weighty contributions. N. I. Pirogov described the examination of the body in his atlas of 1846; in his works on gunshot wounds he also gave information important for examination. In the 20th century, especially after the Second World War, scientific research intensified, and many textbooks and manuals were produced.

t: Early knowledge in Central Asia and Uzbekistan
n: Early knowledge in Central Asia and Uzbekistan. Until the beginning of the 20th century, justice in this region was administered according to the rules of Sharia, and the involvement of medical representatives was not provided for. Nevertheless, the works of Beruni, Ibn Sina and Ismail Jurjani contain information relevant to forensic medicine. In the "Canon of Medicine", Ibn Sina wrote about postmortem changes, types of violent death, poisons and injuries; his aim was correct medical care.

Forensic medicine departments in Uzbekistan. Scientific research from the 1920s is linked with the work of departments of higher medical schools. The first department was opened in 1920 in the medical faculty of Turkestan University. Then departments were opened in Samarkand in 1935, in Andijan in 1959, and in the Tashkent Paediatric Institute in 1972. In 1993 a course was organised at the Tashkent Institute for the Advanced Training of Physicians; now there are courses at 9 forensic medicine departments in higher medical education.

t: The expert service: place and tasks
n: The place and tasks of the expert service. Forensic medical examination is a specialised branch of the health-care system, whose task is to resolve medico-biological questions in criminal and civil cases. The institutions also carry out measures to improve the quality of medical care and to prevent trauma, poisoning and sudden death. In the formation of the service, 4 periods are conventionally distinguished.

The first and second periods. The first period lasted until the 1920s: according to the statute of 1842, hospital physicians were the first instance, in complex cases the second instance, and in especially complex cases a medical council. In Turkestan until the 1920s there was no expert-criminalistic institution, and examinations were carried out sporadically. In the second period, until the 1950s, examinations were carried out mainly in departments; in 1945 the "Republican Forensic Medical Examination Office" was opened in Tashkent.

The third and fourth periods. In the third period, 1950–1991, the Chief Bureau of Forensic Medical Examination of the Ministry of Health was established in 1950 and bureaus were opened in the regions. The bureaus had units for examination of dead bodies, of living persons, and laboratory examination. The fourth period begins in 1991: the service became independent, the Law "On Forensic Examination" was adopted for the first time, and a system of personnel training and attestation was created.

t: Mechanical injuries: the concept of bodily injury
n: Mechanical injuries and the concept of bodily injury. Forensic traumatology deals with determining the mechanism and time of injury, establishing the object that caused it, and the forensic evaluation of the injury. Disturbance of the integrity or function of organs and tissues as a result of an external action that led to impairment of health or death is called bodily injury. If the disturbance arose from an internal action, it is understood as disease.

Classification of damaging factors. There are four types of external action: physical, chemical, biological and psychic. Studying the results of psychic action is the subject of forensic psychiatry. Varieties of physical action include mechanical, thermal, electrical, barometric and radiation factors. Mechanical factors include blunt and sharp objects and firearms. The thermal factor is high and low temperature, the barometric factor is high and low pressure, the electrical factor is technical and atmospheric current, and the radiation factor is X-rays and isotopes.

Classification of injuries. An injury produced by one factor is called simple, and one produced by two or more types is called combined. If it lies in one anatomical region, the injury is isolated; if in two or more regions, it is multiple by region. By number, single and multiple injuries are distinguished. Example: a stab wound of the chest is a simple, isolated, single injury.

The place of mechanical injuries. Mechanical injuries hold the leading place in the examination of dead bodies and living persons. In recent years, among causes of death they rank after cardiovascular and oncological diseases. Anatomical injuries include abrasion, bruise, wound, fracture and dislocation. Functional injuries include shock, concussion and aspiration asphyxia.

Types of trauma. A set of similar injuries observed in a group of persons with the same working and living conditions is called traumatism. Its types are: industrial, transport, military, street, sports, school and domestic traumatism. Most injuries are related to failure to observe rules, including alcohol and drug use.

Vitality of injuries. Establishing vitality is important, because after death an injury may be inflicted deliberately or accidentally, for example during resuscitation, transportation or by animals. General signs: external and internal bleeding, aspiration, myoglobin, embolism and erythrophagia. Local signs: haemorrhage, thrombus, reactive oedema, inflammation, muscle contraction and necrosis.

Methods of examining injuries. An injury is first examined macroscopically: the type, site, shape, colour, ends, edges and floor of the wound are studied, and measurements are made. Clinicians must describe the injury fully, because without a full description serious difficulty arises in carrying out the tasks of the examination. Additional methods: radiography, colour prints, spectral analysis, stereomicroscopy and traceology. Vitality and age are determined histologically.

Mechanical injury and means. The main condition for the formation of an injury is motion; the severity of the injury is directly proportional to the mass and velocity of the moving factor. Means are of three kinds: a weapon, for example a pistol, rifle or dagger; a tool, for example an axe, saw or scissors; and an object, for example a stone or stick. Mechanical injuries are divided into those inflicted by blunt objects, by sharp objects and by firearms.

t: Primary causes of death from mechanical injury (1–3)
n: Primary causes of death from mechanical injury. A primary cause leads to death at the time of injury or shortly after; a secondary cause, after some time. First cause: injuries incompatible with life, for example separation of the head or division of the body in two. Second cause: injuries of vital organs, for example contusion of the brain and heart. Third cause: blood loss, in which not only the volume but also the rate is important.

Blood loss. With injury of large arteries, even with a loss of up to 500 ml of blood, death in the first minutes may result from ventricular fibrillation. In acute blood loss, band-like haemorrhages under the endocardium of the left ventricle are typical; they are called Minakov spots. Massive blood loss, that is, more than 50 %, 2.5 l or more, occurs more slowly, over several hours. In this case cadaveric lividity appears late and is scanty.

t: Traumatic shock and compression of organs
n: Traumatic shock and compression of organs. Traumatic shock is a response reaction in the form of a serious disturbance of the activity of the central nervous, cardiovascular and endocrine systems. Usually severe, grade III–IV shock leads to death. Another cause: compression of the brain, heart and lungs by blood and air. Examples are haematomas, haemopericardium, and pneumothorax and haemothorax.

Air embolism may develop in injury of large veins and in criminal abortion. A small amount of air, 5–7 cm³, may not lead to dangerous consequences; if 10 cm³ or more enters rapidly, fibrillation and death occur. To detect it, the examination begins with the chest. Water is poured in to cover the heart, and the wall of the right ventricle is punctured. If bubbles emerge through the pericardial water, the result is positive; this is the Sunsov test.

t: Fat embolism, aspiration and secondary causes
n: Fat embolism is seen in fractures of long tubular bones; death occurs after 2–3 days, and the fat stains with Sudan III and Sudan IV. In injury of the larynx and airways, and in fractures of the skull base and nasal bones, asphyxia may result from aspiration of blood. Secondary causes include infectious complications: sepsis, peritonitis, meningitis, osteomyelitis and tetanus. Intoxication and secondary blood loss are also secondary causes.

t: Blunt objects and the contact surface
n: Blunt objects and the contact surface. Injuries from blunt objects make up more than 80 % of examinations of living persons and nearly half of violent deaths. Objects may be hard, for example a stone or stick; soft, for example a scarf; or elastic, for example a rubber ball. The injury may be direct or indirect. The contact surface is limited or unlimited; the relative surface is compared with the surface of the injured region.

Impression and inertial trauma. If the mass of the object is less than the mass of the injured region, impression trauma results; the injury is confined to the area of action. If the force of action is much greater than the mass of the region or body, inertial, that is, acceleration, trauma occurs. In inertial trauma, indirect injuries and general concussion are found, and in craniocerebral injuries, contrecoup injuries.

t: Mechanisms of action: impact, compression, tension
n: Mechanisms of action: impact, compression and tension. Impact is a brief action directed to one side. In compression, two forces act for a long time toward each other; the injury of internal organs and bones is then more serious than the external injury. In tension, the forces act away from the centre: lacerated wounds, ruptures and separation of body parts result. Tension also takes part in bite wounds.

Friction, torsion and shaking. In friction, only direct injuries are produced, mainly abrasions. In torsion, mainly indirect injuries are seen: spiral fractures of bones. In shaking, a weak action produces concussion of the brain; a strong action produces injury of the internal organs and ligaments. The "shaken baby syndrome" is also based on precisely the shaking mechanism.

Abrasion. An abrasion is a breach of the integrity of the epidermis and the papillary layer of the dermis; it is divided into superficial, that is, epidermis only, and deep. Linear abrasions are called scratches; at an acute angle the area of friction increases and an arc shape forms. According to Taykov, 1951, 4 stages are distinguished: fresh, up to 12 hours; crust formation, 2–3 days; epithelialisation, 7–9 days; trace, 10–15 days.

Significance of abrasion. An abrasion confirms mechanical action and allows the mechanism and age to be determined. From its site, shape and number, the circumstances of the event can be surmised; for example, an arc-shaped abrasion on the neck occurs in manual strangulation. On a dead body, an abrasion must be distinguished from the postmortem drying sign, that is, parchment spots: parchment spots are yellow-brown and no crust forms.

Bruises. A bruise is haemorrhage into the skin, subcutaneous fat and soft tissues from rupture of blood vessels; swelling, local rise of temperature and pain are seen. Collection of blood in the tissue spaces or a cavity is called a haematoma. With an object of unlimited surface, the bruise is round or oval. With an object of limited surface, the shape of the bruise resembles the surface of the object.

t: Colour of a bruise and distinction from cadaveric lividity
n: Change in the colour of a bruise is observed over time. In the first days it is reddish-bluish; a green tinge begins to appear at 3–4 days, and a yellow one at 6–8 days. The colour change begins from the peripheral parts; these times are approximate. Haemorrhages in the eye, the lip mucosa and the neck do not change colour, but only pale and disappear.

Wounds from a blunt object. A wound is a division of all layers of the skin and the deep soft tissues; superficial and deep wounds are distinguished. Impact and compression produce a contused wound, strong action a crush wound, impact and tension a lacerated wound, and impact at an acute angle a flap wound. General features: the edges are uneven, with abrasion and haemorrhage; tissue "bridges" lie between the walls; external bleeding is not heavy.
